lines.text: How did we learn that the air around us traps heat, and what did the world do about it? This is the story of climate change, from the first experiments to today.
It starts with Joseph Fourier, a French mathematician fascinated by how heat moves. He wondered why the Earth stays as warm as it does.
In 1856 an American, Eunice Newton Foote, showed that carbon dioxide traps the sun's heat. For years, others got the credit.
In Ireland, John Tyndall measured how gases such as carbon dioxide and water vapour soak up heat, the first clear proof of a greenhouse effect.
In 1896 the Swedish chemist Svante Arrhenius worked it out by hand: burning coal could add enough carbon dioxide to warm the whole planet.
Meanwhile the Serbian scientist Milutin Milankovic explained the ice ages, by slow changes in the tilt and orbit of the Earth.
In 1938 an English engineer, Guy Stewart Callendar, made a bolder claim. Coal and oil, he said, were already warming the planet.
Syukuro Manabe would go on to build the first computer models of the climate, work that later won him a Nobel Prize.
James Hansen, a NASA scientist, would one day carry the warning from the laboratory to the halls of government.
And Al Gore, a future vice president, would spend decades telling the public what the science meant.
In 1958 Charles David Keeling began measuring carbon dioxide on a Hawaiian volcano. His line has climbed year after year, ever since.
By 1970 concern for the planet had become a movement, and the first Earth Day brought millions out in the United States.
The next year activists sailed from Vancouver to protest nuclear tests. Their group, Greenpeace, became known for bold action at sea.
In 1972 the United Nations held its first meeting on the environment, in Stockholm, and set up a programme to protect it.
That same year a report built on computer models warned that endless growth on a finite planet could end in collapse.
In 1987 the world agreed to phase out the chemicals eating the ozone layer. It worked, and it showed that global action was possible.
A year later the United Nations created the IPCC, where thousands of scientists review the research and report to governments.
In 1992 almost every country signed a climate convention, promising to meet each year to cut greenhouse gases.
It was agreed at the Earth Summit in Rio de Janeiro, the meeting behind every climate summit since.
In 1997 the Kyoto Protocol set the first binding limits on emissions for wealthy countries, though some of the biggest emitters stayed out.
A year later came the hockey stick, a thousand years of temperature, flat for centuries and then shooting up.
In 2003 a girl was born in Sweden who would one day sit outside parliament with a sign: Greta Thunberg.
That summer a heatwave swept Europe and killed about seventy thousand people, changing how countries plan for heat.
In 2006 Al Gore's talks became a film, An Inconvenient Truth. It won an Oscar and reached millions.
The same year a British report argued that acting early would cost far less than the damage of doing nothing.
But in 2009 the Copenhagen summit failed to agree a binding treaty, a low point for climate talks.
In 2015 the world tried a new way. In the Paris Agreement, each country set its own targets, and promised to raise them over time.
Two years later the United States said it would leave the agreement, and it said so again in 2025.
In 2018 Extinction Rebellion began in Britain, blocking roads and bridges to demand faster action.
That year Greta Thunberg started her school strike. By 2019 millions of young people had joined her in the streets.
Scientists made the stakes plain: two degrees of warming would be far worse than one and a half, and emissions had to halve by 2030.
In Australia, the Black Summer brought the worst bushfire season on record, burning more than twenty million hectares.
In 2019 the European Union set out its Green Deal, a plan to make Europe climate neutral by mid century.
From 2021 the IPCC's sixth report left no doubt: humans have warmed the planet, unequivocally.
That year in Glasgow, countries agreed for the first time to phase down coal.
In 2022 floods put a third of Pakistan under water.
That same year the United States passed its largest ever investment in clean energy and electric cars.
In Dubai in 2023, countries agreed for the first time to move away from fossil fuels.
Then 2024 became the hottest year ever measured, the first full year more than one and a half degrees warmer than before industry.
In 2025 the talks came to Belem, on the edge of the Amazon rainforest.
The science has been clear for a long time. What happens next is still being written.
